text: A playbook is a defined, automated sequence of steps that runs whenever a specific type of alert comes in. If the last lesson was about what SOAR can do in general, a playbook is where one specific version of that gets written out and actually run -- a repeatable recipe: when this trigger happens, do this step, then this one, branching based on what each step finds.

Take a scenario every SOC deals with constantly: a user forwards a suspicious email. A phishing-report playbook extracts the sender address and any URLs from the email, checks them against threat intel feeds, then branches: if confirmed malicious, it auto-quarantines the email from every inbox it reached and notifies the user who reported it; if inconclusive, it routes the email to an analyst for manual review instead.

Every one of those steps is something an analyst could do by hand, and before SOAR, that's exactly what happened every single time a report came in. The playbook doesn't invent a new capability -- it runs the same decision tree automatically, in seconds, instead of an analyst repeating it manually for the fortieth time that week.

A playbook only works because every branch of its decision tree was already known in advance -- a human already decided, ahead of time, that quarantining is the correct response to a confirmed-malicious verdict. That's the real requirement: the scenario has to be repeatable, happening often enough to be worth automating, and well-understood, meaning every reasonable outcome already has a known correct response.

A genuinely novel incident has neither. There's no pre-agreed decision tree, because nobody has faced exactly this situation before, and forcing a playbook onto it risks a confident, fully automated wrong action. That's why playbooks stay scoped to the repeatable slice of the workload, and why novel investigation stays an analyst's job -- exactly where the next lesson picks up.
